analysis.one_liner: Requires Congress to vote approval before any major federal regulation can take effect.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 232-183 on August 2, 2013, but the Senate never voted, and it died when that Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: Today, a major federal rule — on clean air, workplace safety, food safety, or financial protection — takes effect unless Congress specifically votes to block it. This bill flips that: any rule with an economic effect of $50 million or more, any EPA rule significantly affecting farms, any Affordable Care Act rule, or any rule imposing a carbon tax would need both the House and Senate to pass a resolution approving it, and the President to sign it, within 70 legislative days. If they don't, the rule dies automatically. Backers called this accountability for Congress's delegation of lawmaking to agencies; critics said it would let a divided Congress quietly kill most major protections by simply doing nothing.
analysis.who_benefits: Regulated industries — energy producers, manufacturers, financial firms — that would face fewer or delayed federal rules, since most major rules would lapse unless a politically divided Congress affirmatively approved each one within 70 days. Congressional majorities would also gain a standing veto over executive-branch rulemaking.

how_it_helps.text: Major rules would take effect only if Congress enacted a joint resolution of approval; if none passed within 70 legislative or session days, the rule would be deemed not approved and would never take effect.

The bill widened the definition of 'major rule' from a $100 million annual economic effect to $50 million, and added EPA rules significantly affecting agricultural entities, any carbon-tax rule, and any Affordable Care Act rule to the category requiring congressional approval.
Resolutions to approve a rule could not be amended at any stage, and expedited procedures forced a Senate vote within 15 session days after committee action — fast-tracking votes to block rules.

Agencies would have to submit detailed cost-benefit analyses, job-impact figures split between public and private sectors, and lists of related rules, and courts could review whether an agency completed the requirements for a rule to take effect.

analysis.who_pays: Everyone who relies on federal rules for clean air and water, safe food, workplace and product safety, and financial protection: any major rule would expire unless both chambers of a divided Congress passed an unamendable approval resolution within 70 legislative days, a bar most rules historically would not clear.

drawbacks.text: The bill's stated rationale is constitutional: Congress has delegated lawmaking to executive agencies and should vote on the rules that carry the force of law, making lawmakers directly accountable for them.

An honest supporter would have to acknowledge that the 70-day default death sentence means most major rules would lapse whenever Congress is divided or simply fails to act — and that no-amendment, expedited procedures were designed to make it easy to stop rules, not to scrutinize them.

The bill specifically defines any carbon-tax rule as 'major' and declares in its purpose section that carbon pricing raises energy costs, signaling that one aim was making climate regulation nearly impossible to adopt.

Congress historically enacts very few congressional-review resolutions of any kind; a requirement to affirmatively approve every major rule would amount to a near-shutdown of significant new regulation, including rules with benefits that exceed their costs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The accountability argument is genuine — rules do carry the force of law without a congressional vote. But the design goes far beyond scrutiny: with a lowered $50 million threshold, automatic death after 70 days, and no-amendment procedures, the practical effect would be that most major health, safety, environmental, and financial rules die whenever Congress is divided or inattentive. The bill reads less like oversight and more like a one-way ratchet against regulation, with a specific trigger aimed at carbon pricing and Affordable Care Act rules.

outcome.mechanism: It passed the House on a mostly party-line vote in August 2013, the Senate referred it to its Homeland Security committee in September, and no vote ever happened before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The House Judiciary Committee reported the bill amended on July 19, 2013, by a 20-9 vote, after the Rules and Budget Committees were discharged.
The House passed the bill on August 2, 2013, by a recorded vote of 232-183, with 226 of 233 Republicans voting yes and only 6 of 200 Democrats joining them.

A Democratic motion to recommit the bill with instructions to add a section titled 'Protecting Jobs, Economic Growth, and the Health and Safety of the American Public' failed 185-229, with all but two Republicans voting no.

The Senate received the bill on September 9, 2013, and referred it to the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which never reported it and where it never received a vote before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because it died in the Senate, the existing system stayed in place: major rules still take effect unless Congress affirmatively blocks them, so federal health, safety, environmental, and financial protections were not moved behind a congressional approval vote. Regulated industries that would have gained that chokepoint did not get it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal protections kept; industry gains denied

sides.party_line_note: The House passage vote split almost entirely by party: 226 of 233 Republicans voted yes, while only 6 of 200 Democrats did (232-183).

industries.industry: Fossil fuel and carbon-intensive energy producers
industries.note: The bill expressly defines any rule imposing a carbon tax as 'major,' meaning a congressional approval vote would be required and unpassed rules would die — a targeted mechanism for keeping carbon pricing off the books. Cheaper compliance for the industry comes at the cost of unchecked emissions affecting the public.

Lowering the 'major rule' threshold to $50 million and requiring an affirmative act of Congress for each such rule would delay or kill most significant federal regulation, shifting costs like pollution and safety risks onto the public.

Agencies would lose the ability to put major rules into effect on their own authority, with courts empowered to review whether they completed the new requirements. That loss of power tracks directly with weaker protections for the people the rules serve.
